newsitem.title: ITALY: Berisha says won't resign, Italy readies aid.
newsitem.headline: Berisha says won't resign, Italy readies aid.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha said in an interview published on Sunday that he would not step down and asked the international community to help his country avert civil war.

The interview in the Rome newspaper La Repubblica was published on the eve of a meeting in Brussels of European Union foreign ministers to work out a blueprint for security measures to assist a major humanitarian relief mission.
On Sunday more Albanian refugees arrived in southern Italy after a lull of three days caused by bad weather.

"I will not submit to blackmail, I will not let myself be frightened by the threat of arms," he was quoted as telling the newspaper's correspondent in Tirana when asked why he was not heeding calls by rebels to step down.
"I have remained here throughout this crisis, at this desk, because this is where I should stay, even if I have seen things that were unheard of," he said.
He added: "My future is in the hands of the Albanian people. I won't leave politics but I will respect, without any hesitation, any decision of the people. This too is democracy."
Berisha, blamed by the rebels for not stopping shady savings schemes in which many Albanians lost their savings, has promised to quit if his party loses new elections to be held by June.
Berisha said he wanted the international community to help Albania "avert civil war and help us put the country back on its feet".

The Italian foreign ministry said its diplomats were working to provide an "immediate and effective" response to the Albanian government's request for aid but that such a mission would necessarily need international protection.
This would have to be decided by the EU foreign ministers on Monday.

Italy was preparing to send emergency health supplies to Albania following a request from Prime Minister Bashkim Fino. The supplies, in the form of health kits, would be enough for 300,000 people for a month. It was not clear when they would be sent.
Fino is due to travel to Rome on Tuesday to discuss the Albanian crisis with EU foreign ministers in the capital to mark the 40th anniversary of the founding of the European Economic Community.
Fino on Saturday rebuffed rebels holding the south of the country by dismissing their calls for Berisha to quit but said he was ready to open a dialogue with them.
In an interview with Reuters, Fino said Berisha's resignation would cause a power vacuum in a country still reeling from weeks of looting and shooting by Albanians angry at the loss of their money.

Fino, a member of the opposition Socialist Party, has been locked in a power struggle with Berisha's Democrats, who control 122 of the 140 seats in parliament after elections last May that international observers said were deeply flawed.
Nerly 11,000 Albanian refugees escaping the chaos in their country have landed in Italy since March 13 in a flotilla of rusty boats the Italian navy and coastguard deem unseaworthy.
After a lull of several days caused by bad weather, more boats arrived in the southern port of Brindisi at the weekend.
A military boat carrying some 130 people arrived early on Sunday and at least one other boat was expected during the day.

Rome and Tirana are negotiating an agreement to allow the Italian navy to patrol within the Balkan country's territorial waters in an effort to stem the exodus and take part in the planned humanitarian operation.
